Quantum Interfaces: transferring quantum information between light and matter

Lecture 2: The platforms, the links and what limits them

Shayne Bennetts

IAMS Yb Lab, Institute of Atomic and Molecular Sciences, Academia Sinica

TIGP, Tuesday 24 November 2026

2.5

Linking nodes: the repeater problem and heralded entanglement

The figures of merit of a link · fibre loss · Briegel's repeater · Hong-Ou-Mandel and the Bell-state measurement · two ways to herald · DLCZ · the link rate · frequency conversion

2.5

The numbers of lecture 1 decide how well a link works

  • C1 or β says how well each node couples to its mode
  • η is the fraction of photons collected, transmitted and detected
  • The rate is the probability per attempt times the attempt rate
  • ηlink=γent/γdec weighs the rate of pairs against the decoherence of the memories
  • A fidelity is quoted with its success probability
Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023)
2.5-1

The symbols are those of lecture 1, unchanged

SymbolMeaning
ΓNatural linewidth, the population decay rate, Γ=1/τ
γ=Γ/2Decay rate of the dipole amplitude
Ω, ΔFull Rabi frequency; detuning Δ=ωL−ω0
gSingle-photon coupling; the vacuum Rabi splitting is 2g
κCavity field decay rate, the half width
C1=g2/(2κγ)Single-atom cooperativity
β=Γ1D/(Γ1D+Γ′)Fraction into the guided mode; β=2C1/(1+2C1)
OD=−lnTOptical depth on resonance; OD≈2Nβ on a waveguide
  • Widths are quoted as Γ/2π; a paper's own value and form follow in brackets
Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), Eqs. 2 and 4
2.5-2

A photon's survival in fibre falls exponentially with length

T=e−L/Latt=10−αL/10
  • α is the fibre loss in dB/km
  • At 854 nm, about 3 dB/km, a photon survives 50 km with probability 10−15
  • At 1550 nm the loss is 0.181 dB/km, but the fall is still exponential
  • The rate of a direct link falls the same way
Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019)
2.5-3

Briegel's repeater swaps and purifies short entangled links

  • Each segment, about one Latt long, is entangled on its own and kept until needed
  • A Bell measurement at a shared node swaps two pairs into one twice as long
  • Purification turns two noisy pairs into one better pair
  • Nested, purify then swap, the resources grow polynomially with distance
  • Local errors at the percent level are tolerated
Briegel, Dür, Cirac and Zoller, Phys. Rev. Lett. 81, 5932 (1998); Żukowski et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 71, 4287 (1993)
2.5-4

Two photons on a beam splitter herald a Bell state

  • Identical photons leave the beam splitter by the same port
  • A D1D2 coincidence projects the photons onto |Ψ−⟩
Hong, Ou and Mandel, Phys. Rev. Lett. 59, 2044 (1987), Fig. 2
2.5-5

Two ways to herald: one click or two photons

  • a: each node is weakly excited, and one click heralds
  • The rate goes as η; the paths must hold to a fraction of λ
  • DLCZ needs δx≤0.1 µm over about 30 s for 10 km links
  • b: a coincidence of two photons heralds |Ψ−⟩
  • The rate goes as η2; the paths must hold to about 0.3 m
  • The path tolerance is about 3×106 times looser than in scheme a
Chen et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 022329 (2007); Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007); Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019)
2.5-6

One click wins at low efficiency, two photons at high

H1=2P×0.1,H2=P2/2
  • P is the probability that one node's photon is detected
  • For one click, each node emits with probability 0.1
  • At P=0.01, H1=0.002 and H2=5×10−5
  • Over 100 km at 2 kHz, that is 4 heralds per second against 0.1
  • Above P=0.4 the two-photon herald wins
Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019)
2.5-7

In DLCZ, one click shares one excitation between two clouds

S†=N−1/2∑i|s⟩i⟨g|
(SL†±eiϕSR†)|0⟩L|0⟩R/2
  • A weak write pulse makes one Stokes photon with probability pc≪1
  • One click heralds one excitation shared by the two clouds
  • Loss leaves the state unchanged and only lengthens the wait, T0~tΔ/(ηppc)
  • With efficient joining, the total time grows as (L/L0)2, not exponentially
Duan, Lukin, Cirac and Zoller, Nature 414, 413 (2001), Eq. 6
2.5-8

The rate of heralded pairs set against their decoherence

P=η2/2,R=f×P×d
ηlink=γent/γdec
Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023); Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007); Hucul et al., Nat. Phys. 11, 37 (2015); van Leent et al., Nature 607, 69 (2022)
2.5-9

The wavelength decides where frequency conversion pays

  • At 369.5 nm the fibre loses about 0.1 dB/m
  • At 854 nm it loses about 3 dB/km, at 1550 nm 0.181 dB/km
  • The dashed curve is 854 nm light converted to 1550 nm with 25 % efficiency
  • For 854 nm, conversion pays beyond the dot, near 2 km
Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007), for 369.5 nm; Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019), for 854 nm, 1550 nm and the conversion
2.5-10
2.6

Trapped ions

Two ions linked through lenses · the rate budget · an ion in a cavity · conversion to 1550 nm · heralded links from 2007 to 2025

2.6

Two ions 1 m apart, entangled by their photons

  • Two 171Yb+ ions 1 m apart send their photons to one beam splitter (b)
  • Each photon carries its qubit in frequency: two colours 12.6 GHz apart (a)
  • A coincidence of the two detectors projects the ions onto |Ψ−⟩
  • The path difference matters only on the scale 2π/Δk = 2.4 cm
  • Heralded F=0.63±0.03, at 2.0×10−3 s−1
Figure: Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007), Fig. 1
2.6-1

Two photons are needed, so the efficiencies enter squared

P=14[12qDζTρPexcε]2≈3.6×10−9
R=fP=2.0×10−3 s−1
  • An ion emits a 369.5 nm photon with probability ρPexc = 0.995 × 0.5
  • The lens collects ε = 0.02 of the solid angle
  • Fibre, optics and detector pass ζ = 0.2, T = 0.8 and qD = 0.15
  • A polariser passes half; a coincidence heralds only |Ψ−⟩, one Bell state of four
  • The attempts are repeated at f=5.5×105 s−1
Moehring et al., Nature 449, 68 (2007), p. 70; its η, ΔΩ/4π and R are written qD, ε and f here
2.6-2

The first ion link faster than its own decoherence

ηlink=RT2≈4.5 s−1×1.12 s≈5
  • Two 171Yb+ modules about 1 m apart, joined at a beam splitter (a)
  • Success probability 9.7×10−6 per attempt at 470 kHz: 4.5 pairs a second
  • Heralded F=0.78±0.03, the mean of the two heralded Bell states
  • Coherence time T2 = 1.12 s under spin echo
Figure: Hucul et al., Nat. Phys. 11, 37 (2015), Fig. 1; ηlink=γent/γdec after Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023)
2.6-3

A cavity node already works at C₁ ≈ 2

C1=g22κγ=1.422×0.05×11.2≈2
  • A 40Ca+ ion sits in a 2 cm cavity at 854 nm, finesse 77 000 (a)
  • (g,κ,γ)=2π×(1.4, 0.05, 11.2) MHz; C1 is calculated from these
  • A bichromatic Raman transition puts the photon into the cavity (b)
  • Ion-photon F = 97.4(2) %, post-selected on a detected photon
  • A photon is detected in 5.7 % of the sequences
Figure: Stute et al., Nature 485, 482 (2012), Fig. 1
2.6-4

The mirror losses, not the coupling, cost the photons

κoutκ=T1T1+T2+ℓ≈0.16
  • The output mirror transmits T1 = 13 ppm, the other T2 = 1.3 ppm
  • The two mirrors lose ℓ = 68 ppm between them
  • So only 16 % of the photons leave through the output mirror (a)
  • The detectors register 40 % of those, 6.4 % in all (b)
  • The paper reports 40.5 detected events per second
Stute et al., Nature 485, 482 (2012); κout/κ as in Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), Eq. 13
2.6-5

Conversion to 1550 nm carries the ion's photon 50 km

  • A 40Ca+ ion in a cavity with C1=1.47±0.03 emits at 854 nm
  • At 854 nm the fibre loses 3 dB/km: 10−15 of the photons survive 50 km
  • The photon is converted to 1550 nm with 25 % efficiency
  • After 50 km, ion-photon F=0.86±0.03, post-selected on a detected photon
  • Success 5.3×10−4 per attempt at 2.2 kHz: about one photon a second
Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019); fibre losses as in section 2.5
2.6-6

Two ions in two buildings, 230 m apart

WindowHeralded F (%)Rate
1 µs88.0−4.7+2.23.5 min−1
Full58.7−2.1+1.70.49 s−1
  • Two 40Ca+ cavity nodes are joined by 520(2) m of fibre (a, b)
  • Each row is one operating point; the 1 µs window post-selects among the heralds
  • A repeater node of the same group sends photons down two 25 km spools
  • Its memory raises the success probability 128 times and decoheres in 62 ± 3 ms (fitted)
Figure: Krutyanskiy et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 050803 (2023), Fig. 1, satellite image Google Earth, Landsat / Copernicus; Krutyanskiy et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 130, 213601 (2023)
2.6-7

Since 2007 heralded ion links gained in rate and fidelity

  • Main 2025: heralded 96.89(8) % at 9.7 s−1, and a deterministic teleported CZ gate at 86.2(9) %
  • Saha 2025: heralded 97.0(4) % at 0.35 s−1
  • O'Reilly 2024, two ions in one trap: heralded at least 93.7(1.3) % at 79(3) s−1
  • With a coolant ion: 250(8) s−1, no F printed
O'Reilly et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 133, 090802 (2024); Main et al., Nature 638, 383 (2025); Saha et al., Nat. Commun. 16, 2533 (2025); earlier points as on slides 2.6-1, 2.6-3 and 2.6-7
2.6-8

Four choices inside an ion link, side by side

ChoiceOne wayThe other way
Lens or cavity0.8 NA lenses, 333 kHz of attempts: 2.4(1)×10−4 per attempt; heralded at least 93.7(1.3) % at 79(3) s−1 (O'Reilly 2024)Cavities at 854 nm: one attempt per 420 µs; heralded 58.7−2.1+1.7 % at 0.49 s−1 (Krutyanskiy 2023)
One species or twoTwo 40Ca+ in one cavity: attempts on one ion cut the other's coherence from 108(1) to 59(1) ms (Krutyanskiy 2023)88Sr+ makes the photons; the 43Ca+ memory keeps a process fidelity of 98.1(4) % and 98.2(5) % (Main 2025)

2.6-9

2.7

Neutral atoms

Cavity and free-space nodes, from one atom to a 33 km link and error-detected gates · waveguides, nanofibre cavities, atom arrays and ensembles

Figure: Fig. 1a of Kato and Aoki, PRL 115, 093603 (2015); Đorđević, Science 373, 1511 (2021); Goban, PRL 115, 063601 (2015); Tiecke, Nature 508, 241 (2014); Zhou, PRL 130, 103601 (2023); Menon, Nat. Commun. 15, 6156 (2024), CC BY 4.0
2.7

The single-atom cooperativity C₁ of neutral-atom cavities

C₁ as in Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), Eq. 4; each value from the paper named in its row, Ozawa 2026 a preprint
2.7-1

Error correction tolerates noisy pairs but consumes many

  • The seam between two modules tolerates about 10 % Bell-pair error at 1 % local error (calculated)
  • Sinclair's threshold point is 8.8 % at 1.1 % local error; Sunami's is 15.3 % at 0.1 %
  • A distance-20 surface code consumes 40 pairs per cycle and 800 per logical gate
  • Encoded first, 86 pairs at 1 % error give one logical pair below 10−10 (calculated)
  • Designs project about 106 pairs per second with one cavity, 5×107 with 30
Ramette et al., npj Quantum Inf. 10, 58 (2024); Sinclair et al., Phys. Rev. Research 7, 013313 (2025); Sunami et al., PRX Quantum 7, 033014 (2026); Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012); van Leent et al., Nature 607, 69 (2022)
2.7-2

Six ways to bring the photon of an atom into a fibre

  • In A to D the atom sits in free space: in a lens's focus, or between mirrors or fibre tips
  • In E and F it sits in the evanescent field, a few hundred nanometres from glass
Distances: Nguyen 2017; Hartung 2024; Ye 2026 (preprint); Shaw 2026; Soper 2026; Grinkemeyer 2025; Samutpraphoot 2020; Đorđević 2021; Kato and Aoki 2015; Nayak 2019
2.7-3

Without a cavity, two atoms are entangled once per 106 s

P=η1η22,R=fPd
  • One excitation gives a click with probability η1=0.9×10−3 or η2=1.25×10−3
  • Hence P=0.56×10−6 per attempt, calculated [the paper's 0.54×10−6]
  • Attempts run at f = 50 kHz, with an atom in both traps a fraction d = 0.35 of the time
  • Heralded fidelity 0.811 and 0.815 (± 0.028) at this rate; S = 2.19 ± 0.09
Hofmann et al., Science 337, 72 (2012)
2.7-4

With conversion, two atoms link over 33 km of fibre

  • The success probability is 3.66×10−6 at 6 km and 1.22×10−6 at 33 km
  • With the reloading of the atoms, that is one heralded event per 19 s and per 208 s
  • The paper's 1/9 and 1/85 s−1 count only the time with both atoms trapped
  • The heralded fidelity is at least 0.830(10) at 6 km and 0.622(15) at 33 km
  • Each atom's memory has a coherence time T2≈330 µs
van Leent et al., Nature 607, 69 (2022)
2.7-5

Ytterbium at 1389 nm reaches fibre without conversion

  • In ¹⁷¹Yb, ³D₁ decays to ³P₀ at 1389 nm, a telecom band, with branching 0.64(1)
  • Atom-photon fidelity 0.90(1) raw and 0.950(9) corrected, on the photons detected
  • About 0.5 % of the photons reach the fibre, and the rate is below 1 Hz
  • Five channels run at a crosstalk of −13.7(4) dB
  • The design gives C1=1.3 [the paper's 2.6]
Li et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 1826 (2025)
2.7-6

One atom in a cavity stores a photon's polarisation

  • Boozer 2007 mapped a pulse of n¯=1.1 into an atom and back with efficiency ζ=0.057
  • Specht 2011 stores weak pulses, n¯<1, as polarisation qubits at C1≈1.7, calculated
  • Writing, storing and reading have an overall efficiency of (9.3 ± 1) %
  • The fidelity is 92.7(2) % after 2 µs, on the retrieved photons, not heralded
  • It beats the bounds of 2/3 (single photons) and 80 % (this input)
Boozer et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 98, 193601 (2007); Specht et al., Nature 473, 190 (2011)
2.7-7

Two single-atom nodes 21 m apart share entanglement

  • Atom A emits a photon into 60 m of fibre and atom B absorbs it (Cirac et al. 1997)
  • State transfer reaches 84(1) % fidelity at 0.2 % success, post-selected
  • Entanglement reaches 85(1.3) % at 2 % success, not heralded
  • Kept to the earliest photons, the fidelity is 98.7(2.2) %, post-selected
  • 100 µs after its creation the entangled state still has a fidelity of 56(3) %
Figure: Ritter et al., Nature 484, 195 (2012), Fig. 1; the transfer: Cirac, Zoller, Kimble and Mabuchi, Phys. Rev. Lett. 78, 3221 (1997)
2.7-8

Six atoms in one cavity yield a photon in 88.6 % of attempts

  • The cavity has C1≈1.7, calculated, the same as in Specht 2011
  • With one atom, atom-photon entanglement reaches 86.6(5) % on the photons detected
  • The efficiency from generation to detection is then 33.2(2) %
  • With six atoms, at least one photon comes out in 88.6(1) % of attempts
Hartung et al., Science 385, 179 (2024)
2.7-9

A 1.67 mm cavity couples 16 atoms at once (preprint)

  • Ye 2026: one atom has C1 = 56.2(1.7) [the paper's 4g2/(κΓ) = 112.3 ± 3.3]
  • Sixteen atoms at the antinodes keep a mean C1 of 47.9(5) [95.7 ± 0.9]
  • The finesse is 9.5×104, and an objective of NA 0.65 looks in from the side
  • An 11 mm near-concentric cavity gave one atom C1 = 0.084(4) (Nguyen 2017)
  • Huie 2021 designs one at 1480 nm for 100 to 200 171Yb atoms, design value C≈16
Figure: Ye et al., arXiv:2607.04090 (2026), preprint, Fig. 1b and 1c; Nguyen et al., Phys. Rev. A 96, 031802(R) (2017); Huie et al., Phys. Rev. Research 3, 043154 (2021), design
2.7-10

Lenses inside a cavity focus its mode far from every surface

  • One atom splits the vacuum Rabi doublet: C1 = 0.8(1) [the paper's 4g2/(κΓ) = 1.6(2)]
  • The light passes the atom about ten times; the optics are mm to cm away
  • The microscope (a) gives each atom its own mode; 21 are read in parallel (b)
  • There C1≈0.8 [1.6(2)] is calculated from finesse and waist, not measured on atoms
  • Without atoms, 603 cavities reach a mean finesse of 114(17)
Figure: Shaw et al., Nature 650, 320 (2026), Fig. 1; Shadmany et al., Sci. Adv. 11, eads8171 (2025); Soper et al., Phys. Rev. X (2026)
2.7-11

A fibre cavity at C₁ = 51 detects errors in two-atom gates

|D⟩=|eg,0⟩−|ge,0⟩2
  • Strong coupling at C1=50.5(1.0) [the paper's 4g2/(κΓ)=101(2), full widths]
  • With one excitation shared, the dark state |D⟩ does not couple to the cavity
  • Carving prepares a Bell state at 91(4) % fidelity and 32(1) % success, heralded
  • The gate alone reaches 52.5(18) %, deterministic
  • Error detection raises it to 76(2) % at 69(1) % success, heralded
Figure: Grinkemeyer et al., Science 387, 1301 (2025), Fig. 1
2.7-12

One guided mode collects a large share of an atom's light

  • A nanofibre gives β≈0.13, calculated
  • The alligator waveguide gives β=0.24 (Γ1D/Γ′=0.32±0.08)
  • Atoms trapped in it reach β≈0.5 (Γ1D/Γ=1.1±0.1)
  • A crystal cavity reaches C1=3.9 (η=7.7±0.3)
  • In it, atom and light shift each other's phase by about π, post-selected
Figures: Tiecke et al., Nature 508, 241 (2014), Fig. 1a (left); Goban et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 063601 (2015), Fig. 1(a) (right); Solano et al., Nat. Commun. 8, 1857 (2017); Goban et al., Nat. Commun. 5, 3808 (2014)
2.7-13

Two atoms in one detuned cavity exchange an excitation

J=g2Δac
  • Δac is the cavity's detuning from both atoms
  • For Δac≫g the cavity photon is only virtual
  • The cavity couples |eg⟩ and |ge⟩ with the strength J
  • As atom 2 is tuned through atom 1, the two states split by 2J
Calculated with J/2π=25 MHz, the value of Samutpraphoot et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 063602 (2020)
2.7-14

Two atoms at a nanophotonic cavity show the splitting 2J

  • At the mode centre one atom has C1=36(2) (the paper's 71(4)), a mean over its motion
  • The two atoms sit 1 µm off centre, where C1=15.5(1.0) (the paper's 31(2))
  • From the mean cooperativity the paper expects J=2π×25(4) MHz
  • Measured (b), the levels repel with the gap 2J=2π×50(8) MHz, as in the model (c)
Figure: Samutpraphoot et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 124, 063602 (2020), Fig. 4
2.7-15

Two atoms are entangled at a cavity, then one is carried away

  • C1=13.5(5) as a thermal mean, 23.5(5) at rest (the paper's 27(1) and 47(1))
  • Carving with a reflected pulse of n¯=0.35 gives F=0.72(3), post-selected
  • After one atom is moved 1 µm in 650 µs, F=0.52(5), post-selected
  • Corrected for atom loss and readout, the moved pair has 0.65(6)
  • The coherence time T2 is 2.1(1) ms at the cavity and 9.7(8) ms in free space
Figure: Đorđević et al., Science 373, 1511 (2021), Figs. 3B, 3C and 4
2.7-16

A nanofibre between two fibre Bragg gratings is a cavity

  • One atom is trapped beside the nanofibre
  • Rates: (g0,κ,γ)/2π=(7.8,6.4,2.6) MHz
  • The 33 cm cavity has a finesse below 40
  • The coupling is strong: g0 exceeds κ and γ
  • The cooperativity is C1=g02/(2κγ)≈1.8
Kato and Aoki, Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 093603 (2015)
2.7-17

One Cs atom at a nanofibre cavity reaches C₁ = 2.7

C=4g02κγ0=5.4±0.6=2C1
  • A tweezer holds one Cs atom about 190 nm from a nanofibre, inside a fibre cavity of finesse 140
  • The paper's κ/2π=164 MHz and γ0/2π=5.2 MHz are full widths; halved, they give C1=C/2=2.7(3), measured
  • g0/2π is 34±2 MHz from the photon statistics and 36±1 MHz from the antibunching
  • With 2g0<κ there is no splitting, and the paper claims no strong coupling
  • The atom emits 85 ± 2 % of its light into the fibre
Nayak, Wang and Keloth, Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 213602 (2019)
2.7-18

171Yb atoms couple to a 1389 nm nanofibre cavity (preprint)

  • g/2π=1.86(17) MHz for one atom, G/2π=3.78(19) MHz for five
  • The atoms stay trapped for 6.8(4) s
  • C1≈2.9 (the paper's internal Cin=5.6(1.0))
  • The calculated maximum of Cin is 14.2
  • An entanglement rate of 40 kHz is projected
Figure: Ozawa et al., arXiv:2609.25232 (2026), preprint, Fig. 1a (top) and Fig. 2 (bottom)
2.7-19

Nanofibre cavities reach C₁ of 2 to 3; designs project far more

  • Kato 2015 and Nayak 2019 measure C1≈1.8 and 2.7(3)
  • The Ozawa 2026 preprint has about 2.9 (internal 5.6(1.0))
  • Designs project 90 and about 150 for an atom 200 nm from the surface
  • At the surface the projection is 1050
  • Chip cavities have measured 13.5 and 36
Kato and Aoki, Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 093603 (2015); Nayak, Wang and Keloth, Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 213602 (2019); Ozawa et al., arXiv:2609.25232 (2026); Horikawa et al., Opt. Lett. 50, 5294 (2025); Ruddell et al., Opt. Lett. 45, 4875 (2020)

2.8

Colour centres in diamond and quantum dots

A narrow, stable line · NV links and their rates · SiV in diamond nanocavities · quantum dots

2.8

Symmetry keeps the SiV line narrow in a nanostructure

  • An emitter in a solid is judged on lecture 1's figures of merit, β or C1
  • For a link, photons from two emitters must be alike to interfere (section 2.5)
  • The SiV− centre is inversion symmetric and has no permanent electric dipole
  • So a stray electric field does not shift its line to first order, and the line stays close to lifetime-limited
  • An electron spin holds the qubit; a nearby nuclear spin can store it
Sipahigil et al., Science 354, 847 (2016); Lodahl, Mahmoodian and Stobbe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 347 (2015)
2.8-1

A decay from A2 entangles the NV spin with a photon

R=fPd
  • The NV centre is excited to A2, which decays to |+1⟩ or |−1⟩
  • The two decays emit light of opposite circular polarisation, σ+ and σ−
  • The photon's polarisation records the spin state: spin and photon are entangled
  • f is the attempt rate, P the probability per attempt, d the duty cycle
  • Togan 2010 had P=10−6 at f=100 kHz: one event per 10 s
Togan et al., Nature 466, 730 (2010), levels after its Fig. 3a
2.8-2

An event-ready herald gave a loophole-free Bell test

  • NV centres in labs 1280 m apart send photons over 1.7 km of fibre at 8 dB/km to C
  • A detection at C heralds that the two spins are entangled
  • About 6.4×10−9 of the attempts succeed: 245 heralded trials in 220 h
  • The Bell parameter was S=2.42±0.20, with p=0.039
  • The heralded spin-spin fidelity is estimated at 0.92 ± 0.03
Hensen et al., Nature 526, 682 (2015)
2.8-3

Two NVs 2 m apart entangle faster than they decohere

ηlink=γent/γdec
  • The bright-state population α trades rate against fidelity
  • Heralded: 0.81(2) at 6 Hz for α=0.05, 0.60(2) at 39 Hz for α=0.3
  • The entangled state decoheres at γdec=5.0(3) Hz (the paper's rdec)
  • The paper quotes ηlink~8; 39 Hz over 5 Hz gives the same
  • Delivered deterministically at α=0.2: 0.56(1) at 9.9 Hz
Humphreys et al., Nature 558, 268 (2018), Fig. 2; Covey, Weinfurter and Bernien, npj Quantum Inf. 9, 90 (2023)
2.8-4

NV links reached 10 km, at far lower rates than over metres

LinkDistanceFidelityRate

2.8-5

In a diamond nanocavity an SiV reached C₁ ≈ 0.5

  • (g,κ,γ)/2π=(2.1, 28.5, 0.15) GHz, as half widths
  • So C1≈0.5 [the paper's 4g2/(κγ)=1.0(1)]
  • With κ≫g the cavity is in the bad-cavity regime
  • The cavity shortens the excited-state lifetime from 1.8 to 0.6 ns
  • Two SiVs in one waveguide reached F≥82(7) %, post-selected, at about 0.5 Hz
Figure: Sipahigil et al., Science 354, 847 (2016), Fig. 1
2.8-6

One SiV makes tunable Raman photons and switches light

  • |u⟩, 64 GHz from |c⟩, misses the cavity
  • The laser tunes the Raman photon over 6 GHz
  • About 15 kHz of single photons, g(2)(0)=0.16(3)
  • One SiV takes 38(3) % of the transmission
  • Pairs pass, single photons scatter: g(2)(0)=1.50(5)
  • At 4 K phonons mix |u⟩ and |c⟩ in about 10 ns
Figure: Sipahigil et al., Science 354, 847 (2016), Fig. 4B and 4C (left), Fig. 3A and 3C (right)
2.8-7

SiV cavities have passed 2C₁ = 1, where r changes sign

r=2C1−12C1+1
  • On resonance r is zero at C1=1/2 and tends to +1 for C1≫1
  • In brackets and as light markers: the papers' 4g2/(κγ), with full widths, which is 2C1
  • Sipahigil 2016 sat at C1≈0.5 [1.0(1)], on the dashed line
  • Bhaskar 2020 reached C1=52±6 [105 ± 11]
  • Knaut 2024's two nodes: C1=6.2(5) and 0.8(4) [12.4(9) and 1.5(8)]
Sipahigil et al., Science 354, 847 (2016); Evans et al., Science 362, 662 (2018); Nguyen et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 123, 183602 (2019); Bhaskar et al., Nature 580, 60 (2020); Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024); Reiserer and Rempe, Rev. Mod. Phys. 87, 1379 (2015), Eq. 16
2.8-8

An SiV memory node beat direct transmission fourfold

  • The middle node is an SiV in a nanocavity, C1=52±6 [the paper's 105 ± 11]
  • Its spin holds the first photon until the second arrives: heralded successes at about 0.1 Hz
  • The key rate is 4.1 ± 0.5 times that of direct transmission, over an emulated loss
  • It exceeds the repeaterless bound with 99.2 % confidence
Figure: Bhaskar et al., Nature 580, 60 (2020), Fig. 2a
2.8-9

Two SiV nodes link electrons and store in 29Si nuclei

  • The electron spin is the communication qubit
  • A 29Si nucleus is the memory, with T2=2.1 s
  • One photon passing both nodes heralds their Bell state
  • At about 16 mHz (μ=0.017), heralded, Φ− reached 0.86(3) and Φ+ 0.74(3)
  • Nucleus-nucleus pairs came at 6 mHz; the photons were converted to 1350 nm at 5.4 %
Figure: Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), Fig. 1, CC BY
2.8-10

The SiV link ran over a 35 km deployed fibre loop

  • Raising μ lifts the heralded rate from 16 mHz to 1.05 Hz; the fidelity falls
  • The state stays entangled, above 0.5, up to 1 Hz
  • The inset shows the heralded Φ− and Φ+, measured at the lowest rate
  • Over the loop: 0.69(7) at 0.23 mHz, heralded, with error detection
  • Bersin 2024: heralded state transfer onto an SiV over 50 km at 87.0 ± 2.5 %
Figure: Knaut et al., Nature 629, 573 (2024), Fig. 2c, CC BY; Bersin et al., PRX Quantum 5, 010303 (2024)
2.8-11

Quantum dots entangle a spin with the photons they emit

  • Coste 2023 used a dot in a micropillar cavity
  • Heralded spin-photon-photon states came at 0.53 MHz at the lens, 0.043 MHz in fibre
  • Spin-photon fidelity ≥ 65 ± 1 %, spin-photon-photon ≥ 59 ± 2 %
  • Meng 2024 used a dot in a waveguide, with β≈90 % and a Purcell factor of 4.2
  • Its spin-photon Bell state reached 76.3(5) %, post-selected, at 1.3 % efficiency end to end
Figures: Coste et al., Nat. Photon. 17, 582 (2023), Fig. 1a (left); Meng et al., Nat. Commun. 15, 7774 (2024), Fig. 1 (right), CC BY-NC-ND
2.8-12
2.9

Superconducting circuits and transducers

Circuit QED · thermal microwave photons · four kinds of transducer · rate and added noise · matching at C = 1 · membranes · piezoelectric nanobeams · electro-optic crystals · Rydberg atoms · the noise map

2.9

A transmon in a resonator reaches strong coupling easily

  • The transmon is an artificial atom with a dipole of about 104ea0
  • The splitting 2g/2π=350MHz far exceeds κ/2π≈800kHz
  • The vacuum Rabi frequency times the cavity lifetime reaches 106
  • A CZ gate on one chip reaches a fidelity of 99.93 %
  • Deterministic remote Bell states reach 78.9 % fidelity at 50 kHz
Blais et al., Phys. Rev. A 69, 062320 (2004), Table 1; Blais, Grimsmo, Girvin and Wallraff, Rev. Mod. Phys. 93, 025005 (2021); Kurpiers et al., Nature 558, 264 (2018); Haroche, Brune and Raimond, Nat. Phys. 16, 243 (2020)
2.9-1

A 5 GHz mode at 300 K holds about 1250 thermal photons

nth=1ehf/kBT−1
  • At 300 K and 5 GHz, nth≈kBT/hf≈1250
  • The circuits run near 10 mK; their photons cannot leave the refrigerator
  • An optical photon at 194 THz has nth≈3×10−14 even at 300 K
  • In Haroche's words, “microwave photons are not ideal information carriers”
  • A transducer moves the quantum state onto an optical photon
Haroche, Brune and Raimond, Nat. Phys. 16, 243 (2020)
2.9-2

Two processors can be joined by a cold cable or by light

  • (a) Without a circulator, Leung 2019 made deterministic Bell states at 79.3 % over a metre
  • Magnard 2020 linked two refrigerators over 5 m
  • Qiu 2024 sent single photons through 64 m of cold aluminium cable with 90.4 ± 0.8 % efficiency
  • Its deterministic Bell pairs reached 94.2 ± 0.6 %, corrected for readout; teleportation 78.3 ± 0.8 %
  • The two chips sat 0.15 m apart in one refrigerator; the cable held 4 % thermal photons
  • (b) A transducer at each end would let light cross kilometres of warm fibre (projected)
Blais, Grimsmo, Girvin and Wallraff, Rev. Mod. Phys. 93, 025005 (2021), pp. 53 and 54; Qiu et al., Sci. Bull. (2024), arXiv:2302.08756; Delaney et al., Nature 606, 489 (2022)
2.9-3

Four kinds of transducer join microwave photons to light

  • In (a), electro-optomechanical, a silicon nitride drum at 1.45 MHz couples to both modes
  • In (b), piezo-optomechanical, a 5.2 GHz phonon carries the excitation to a photonic crystal
  • In (c), electro-optic, the microwave field changes the index of lithium niobate directly
  • In (d), cold 85Rb atoms sit in both a 100 GHz cavity and a 780 nm cavity
Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022); Mirhosseini et al., Nature 588, 599 (2020); Sahu et al., Science 380, 718 (2023); Kumar et al., Nature 615, 614 (2023)
2.9-4

A transducer is judged by its photon rate and its added noise

rate=ηt×bandwidth×duty cycle
Nadd=Nout/ηt<1
  • The rate should keep pace with the clock of the system it serves
  • 2 kHz at 50 %, run continuously, matches 20 MHz at 10 % with a duty cycle of 6×10−4
  • Nadd is the added noise referred to the input, in signal photons
  • Pumps couple each mode to the motion at Γe and Γo; a bath of nth phonons heats it
Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022)
2.9-5

Loss alone puts a floor under a transducer's total noise

nin=Nadd+nqnq=12|1−1/ηt|
  • Each grey line is one total noise nin; at ηt=10−3 it is at least 500
  • A perfect transducer, ηt=1 and Nadd=0, sits at the lower right
Caves, Phys. Rev. D 26, 1817 (1982); Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022)
2.9-6

A pump on a sideband swaps or squeezes light and motion

G=g0ncη=4CeCo(1+Ce+Co)2
  • A red-sideband pump swaps light and motion and cools the motion at 4G2/κ
  • A blue-sideband pump makes photon-phonon pairs, two-mode squeezing
  • The cooperativity is C=4G2/(κγm), with κ and γm full widths
  • The swap is quantum when C exceeds the thermal occupation nth
  • A transducer couples the motion to a microwave mode (Ce) and an optical mode (Co)
Dong, Wang and Wang, Natl. Sci. Rev. 2, 510 (2015); Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022)
2.9-7

At C = 1 a converter is matched, not strongly coupled

η=4C(1+C)2=8C1(1+2C1)2
  • The efficiency reaches one at C=1 in full widths, that is C1=1/2
  • This is impedance matching, not strong coupling
  • With three modes (b), the peak η=Co/(1+Co) lies at Ce=1+Co
Dong, Wang and Wang, Natl. Sci. Rev. 2, 510 (2015); Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022)
2.9-8

Membrane transducers cut the added noise to 3.2 photons

Device and settingEfficiencyAdded noise (photons)
Andrews 2014, at 4 K8.6 ± 0.7 %, measuredabout 1500 (Higginbotham 2018)
Higginbotham 2018, peak efficiency47 ± 1 %, measurednot measured, cavity unstable
Higginbotham 2018, feedforward43 %, measured38, measured
Brubaker 2022, peak efficiency47 ± 1 %, measuredmore than 3.2
Brubaker 2022, least noiseless than 47 %3.2 ± 0.1, measured
  • Brubaker's membrane was at 70 ± 10 mK, and the device ran continuously
  • From 2018 to 2022 the added noise fell from 38 to 3.2 photons
  • At a third setting Brubaker's membrane held 0.34 phonons
Andrews et al., Nat. Phys. 10, 321 (2014), Fig. 3b; Higginbotham et al., Nat. Phys. 14, 1038 (2018), Figs. 2c and 4d; Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022)
2.9-9

Cooling the membrane sets how low the added noise goes

  • At the least-noise setting Ce≈1200 (calculated) and nth≈1000
  • Microwave damping alone would leave about nth/Ce≈1 phonon
  • The membrane holds nm=1.5 phonons, which add 1.0 of the 3.2 photons
  • Ground-state cooling of the membrane is “necessary and sufficient” for Nadd<1
Figure: Brubaker et al., Phys. Rev. X 12, 021062 (2022), Fig. 1a, CC BY 4.0
2.9-10

A membrane transducer read a transmon without harming it

  • Delaney 2022 read a transmon optically without destroying its state
  • T2 was 20.7±0.2 µs with the laser on and 20.4±0.2 µs with it off
  • The microwave pump added (3±1)×10−3 photons to the qubit's readout cavity
  • The single-shot readout fidelity was about 0.4, at a quantum efficiency ηq≈8×10−4
  • From the qubit's cavity the chain transmitted 1.9×10−3 and added 740 photons
Figure: Delaney et al., Nature 606, 489 (2022), Fig. 3a
2.9-11

A nanobeam turned a transmon's excitation into light

  • Mirhosseini 2020 put a transmon's excitation into a 5.2 GHz phonon
  • A laser made it a 1541.7 nm photon, at ηt=(0.88±0.16)×10−5
  • The added noise was Nadd=0.57±0.2; the readout was destructive, at 100 Hz
  • Meesala 2024 heralded microwave-optical pairs at 0.14 Hz, with no qubit
Figure: Mirhosseini et al., Nature 588, 599 (2020), Fig. 1e; Meesala et al., Nat. Phys. 20, 871 (2024)
2.9-12

Electro-optic transducers entangled light and drove a qubit

  • Sahu 2023 measured 0.72−0.25+0.31 dB of deterministic two-mode squeezing (2σ)
  • Its fitted cooperativity is C=0.18±0.01 (full widths, 2σ)
  • Warner 2025 drove a transmon with a microwave tone made from two laser tones
  • Its efficiency was ηt=1.18 % on the chip, over a bandwidth of 30 MHz
  • The light gave its microwave resonator fewer than 0.12 noise photons
Figure: Sahu et al., Science 380, 718 (2023), Fig. 1; Warner et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 831 (2025)
2.9-13

Cold atoms convert 100 GHz photons into 780 nm light

  • 85Rb atoms sit where a niobium cavity at 100 GHz crosses a 780 nm cavity, at 5 K
  • The internal efficiency is 58(11) %, over a bandwidth of 360(20) kHz
  • The added noise, 0.6 photons, is the thermal occupation of the 100 GHz mode at 5 K
  • End to end the efficiency is about 2.5 %, limited by the weak out-coupling at 100 GHz
  • Transmons work near 5 GHz; the paper proposes higher Rydberg states in larger, colder cavities
Figure: Kumar et al., Nature 615, 614 (2023), Fig. 1a and 1c
2.9-14

Four fields close a loop through two Rydberg states

𝐤297+𝐤mm=𝐤780+𝐤481
  • A 297 nm laser drives 5S1/2→35P1/2, detuned by Δ
  • A 100 GHz photon from the cavity completes the step to 36S1/2
  • A 481 nm laser takes the atom to 5P3/2, which emits 780 nm light into the cavity
  • The emission is collective only when the four wave vectors close the loop
  • The efficiency peaks near Δ/2π≈4 MHz, where the conversion is matched
Kumar et al., Nature 615, 614 (2023), Fig. 1a, Fig. 3a and Methods
2.9-15

Heat and noise from the pumps limit today's transducers

  • Light breaks Cooper pairs; Mirhosseini's qubit took about 8 ms to recover
  • A 244 mW pulse raised Sahu's microwave bath from 0.03 ± 0.01 to 0.09 ± 0.03 photons
  • Microwave-pump noise is “the major factor preventing quantum-enabled transduction”
  • Warner's cables and circulators to the qubit lost 46 % of the signal
  • Wehner wants a converter over 50 % efficient with a signal-to-noise ratio over 100
  • A heralded pair source keeps its fidelity when photons are lost (Meesala 2024)
Figure: Sahu et al., Science 380, 718 (2023), Fig. 2d; Delaney et al., Nature 606, 489 (2022); Warner et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 831 (2025); Wehner, Elkouss and Hanson, Science 362, eaam9288 (2018); Meesala et al., Phys. Rev. X 14, 031055 (2024)

2.10

2.10-2

Link rates fall by orders of magnitude over distance

R=fPd,P=η2/2
  • The rate is the attempt rate f times the probability per attempt P times the duty cycle d
  • With a two-photon herald P=η2/2: the collection efficiency η enters squared
  • Yu 2020 is not plotted, since its 1.5 Hz at 50 km is an estimate
  • The rate of van Leent 2022 is averaged over the run, reloading included
Data: the papers of slides 2.10-1 and 2.10-2; P=η2/2: Krutyanskiy et al., npj Quantum Inf. 5, 72 (2019)
2.10-3

A repeater can use remote pairs with per-cent errors

  • Local CZ gates reach 99.93 % in superconducting circuits and 99.5 % in tweezer arrays
  • A repeater tolerates remote Bell pairs with errors of several per cent
  • Recent analyses put the tolerated error at 8.8 %, about 10 % and about 13 %
  • Main 2025, 96.89(8) %, heralded, at 9.7 s−1 over 2 m, is the one remote pair below them
Blais, Rev. Mod. Phys. 93, 025005 (2021); Evered, Nature 622, 268 (2023); Briegel, Phys. Rev. Lett. 81, 5932 (1998); Sinclair, Phys. Rev. Research 7, 013313 (2025); Ramette, npj Quantum Inf. 10, 58 (2024); Main, Nature 638, 383 (2025)
2.10-4

Each transition of ytterbium serves a different task

  • The broad 399 nm line loads the atoms, the narrow 556 nm line cools them
  • The metastable ³P₀ and ³P₂ states hold the memory
  • The 1389, 1480 and 1539 nm lines, from ³P up to ³D, lie in the telecom band
  • The ground state ¹S₀ of ¹⁷¹Yb has two nuclear-spin sublevels, split only by a field
Takasu, Phys. Rev. Lett. 93, 123202 (2004); Xu, Phys. Rev. Lett. 113, 033003 (2014); Porsev and Derevianko, Phys. Rev. A 69, 042506 (2004); Beloy, Phys. Rev. A 86, 051404(R) (2012); Li, Nat. Phys. 21, 1826 (2025); Huie, Phys. Rev. Research 3, 043154 (2021); NIST ASD
2.10-5

A linewidth is the sum of the partial decay rates

Γ=∑jΓj,bj=Γj/Γ
  • ³D₁ lives τ = 329.3 ± 7.1 ns, so its linewidth is Γ/2π = 483(10) kHz
  • Its partial rate into ³P₀ is 309(8) kHz, a branching ratio b = 0.64(1)
  • The 1389 nm line is therefore 483 kHz wide, not 309 kHz
  • C1 takes γ=Γ/2 from the full width; the photon into ³P₀ carries b
  • A nanofibre pulled in an H₂–O₂ flame loses 8 % at 1389 nm, in a D₂–O₂ flame under 1 %
Beloy et al., Phys. Rev. A 86, 051404(R) (2012) (lifetime); Li et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 1826 (2025) (partial rates, branching); Horikawa et al., Opt. Lett. 50, 5294 (2025) (OH absorption)
2.10-6

On a nanofibre, one stored photon needs thousands of atoms

β=Γ1DΓ1D+Γ′,C1=Γ1D2Γ′
1−η≈5.8/OD,OD≈2Nβ
  • The lab's design value Γ1D/Γ′ = 0.05 gives C1 = 0.025 and β≈0.048
  • Measured nanofibres give β=OD/2N of 0.3 to 2 %
  • At 0.05, a 1 % storage error needs about 6000 atoms
  • In theory an ordered array of other spacing and coupling errs by 0.15e−N/23
Gorshkov et al., Phys. Rev. A 76, 033805 (2007); Vetsch et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 104, 203603 (2010); Han et al., arXiv:2509.22958 (2025), preprint; Pache et al., Phys. Rev. A 112, L011701 (2025); Asenjo-Garcia et al., Phys. Rev. X 7, 031024 (2017), Fig. 18
2.10-7

The cavity architectures reach C₁ from about 2 to 50

  • Fibre Fabry-Pérot: 50.5(1.0) [101(2)], Grinkemeyer 2025
  • Photonic crystal: 13.5(5) [27(1)], thermal mean, Đorđević 2021
  • Nanofibre: about 1.8, measured, Kato and Aoki 2015
  • Nanofibre: 5.6(1.0) internal, Ozawa 2026, preprint; 90 projected, Horikawa 2025
  • In brackets: the paper's own 4g2/(κγ), with full widths
The lab's nanofibre cavity: picture to come
Grinkemeyer et al., Science 387, 1301 (2025); Đorđević et al., Science 373, 1511 (2021); Kato and Aoki, Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 093603 (2015); Ozawa et al., arXiv:2609.25232 (2026), preprint; Horikawa et al., Opt. Lett. 50, 5294 (2025)
2.10-8

The IAMS lab puts ytterbium in tweezers beside a nanofibre

  • Each ¹⁷¹Yb atom sits in a tweezer at a chosen place in the nanofibre's evanescent field
  • The ³P₀ state is the memory; the photons, at 1389 nm, are in the telecom band
Picture: the IAMS ytterbium lab; 1389 nm: Li et al., Nat. Phys. 21, 1826 (2025); Ozawa et al., arXiv:2609.25232 (2026), preprint; Horikawa et al., Opt. Lett. 50, 5294 (2025)
